fetched_contents.text: Selective leaching of molybdenum from spent hydrodesulphurisation catalysts using ultrasound and microwave methods Introduction Hydrodesulphurisation (HDS) catalysts are extensively used in the petroleum refining industry; during operation, they are deactivated by the deposition of carbon, sulphur and metals (V, Fe, Zn, and As) (Lai et al., 2008, Marafi and Stanislaus, 2008). After continuous activity and intermediate regeneration operations, these catalysts become solid wastes, which are classified as hazardous materials (Rapaport, 2000). The quantity of spent non-reusable hydrodesulphurisation spent catalysts produced per year is around 120,000 tons (dry basis) (Dufresne 2007). Due to strict legislation, the land disposal of these residues, which was practiced in the past, is no longer advisable. Mo is the active metal of such catalysts, typically combined with Co and/or Ni on an alumina carrier. The composition of spent catalysts is mainly Al (15–30%), Mo (4–12%), Ni (1–5%), Co (0–4%), carbon and sulphur (Park et al., 2006); however, the composition depends on the characteristics of the initial catalyst and of the crude oil treated. The presence of valuable metals, largely used in the steel industry and in the manufacture of alloys in addition to their usage in the production of hydrotreating catalysts (Braithwaite and Haber, 1994, Zeng and Cheng, 2009) makes the recovery of metals from spent catalysts the most economical and environmentally attractive solution as both the exploitation of primary mineral resources and the deposition of hazardous wastes are reduced. For this purpose, metal recovery industrial processes have been developed based on pyrometallurgical, hydrometallurgical or a combination of both processes. Although pyrometallurgical operations are usually less expensive, faster and provide higher metal recoveries, the release of harmful gases during smelting and the extremely high temperatures (> 1000 °C) required are not economically compensated when treating low-grade metals, and are important drawbacks when recycling spent catalysts (Ghosh and Ray, 1991, Kim et al., 2009a). Alternatively, hydrometallurgical processes allow better control on the recovery of by-products, are theoretically more environmentally friendly and use lower temperatures; however, some reagents are expensive, reaction rates are much slower and large quantities of concentrated solutions are required (Ghosh and Ray, 1991, Kim et al., 2009a). Several studies have been performed regarding the leaching of the spent HDS catalysts with aqueous solutions: direct leaching with concentrated sulphuric acid and leaching with prior sulphuric acid baking (Kim et al., 2009a, Kim et al., 2009b), extraction of metals with mixtures of strong acids as leaching solutions (Lai et al., 2008) and sulphuric acid leaching of a pre-oxidised catalyst (Valverde et al., 2008) are particular examples. These studies demonstrated that leaching spent catalysts in acidic medium under appropriate conditions leads to greater than 90% Mo, Al and Ni or Co extraction. These procedures use concentrated acids, which require large amounts of reagents to neutralise the leaching solution and, moreover, the extraction is not selective. On the other hand, alkaline leaching allows the selective extraction of Mo over Ni or Co through the use of a sodium hydroxide solution for the first leaching step and sulphuric acid to recover Ni or Co during the second stage (Angelidis et al., 1995). Recent reviews have been published on this subject (Marafi and Stanislaus, 2008, Zeng and Cheng, 2009). In recent years, intensive research on this matter evidenced the need to find a cost-effective and environmentally friendly process to treat spent HDS catalysts. In the last two decades, the application of ultrasound to increase chemical reaction rates underwent an abrupt increase (Capelo-Martínez, 2009). In solid–liquid systems, the incidence of high frequency ultrasonic waves leads to a succession of expansion and compression cycles; consequently, cavitation bubbles are created. The collapse of these bubbles forms high-speed micro-jets toward the solid phase, resulting in erosion and cracking on the surface of the solid; this phenomenon allows better penetration of the liquid into the solid and, thus, enhances the solubilisation of the target metals (Luque de Castro and Priego Capote, 2006). Although ultrasound-assisted extraction of metals has been highly focused on biological materials, like plant tissues and biological samples (Junior et al., 2006, Moreda-Pineiro et al., 2009), some extraction and leaching experiments have already been done for non-biological samples, such as ores and industrial residues. Copper leaching from copper oxide ore with an ammoniacal solution (Rao et al., 1997), acid dissolution of metals from copper slag (Bese, 2007), extraction of manganese from slag using acidic medium (Li et al., 2008) and the separation of copper and iron from printed circuit board sludge (Xie et al., 2009) are examples of experimental studies where ultrasonic techniques have been applied to dissolve metals. These experiments have shown an improvement in metal extraction from solids, either with higher extraction percentages and/or faster dissolution when sonification was applied. These results showed that ultrasound may be an important tool in the future of the metal extraction industry due to the minimisation of energy use and optimisation of the control of chemical reactions. Very recently, the ultrasound-assisted leaching, using an acid solution, was applied to a spent HDS catalyst by Marafi and Stanislaus (2011) and to a nickel spent catalyst by Oza et al. (2011). Every year large quantities of spent hydroprocessing catalysts containing high concentrations of metals such as Mo, V, Ni, and Co are discarded as solid wastes from the petroleum refining industries. The metals present in the spent catalysts can be leached by water and pollute the environment. As these catalysts are hazardous wastes, landfills or other treatment methods for disposal are not preferable when all costs and liabilities are taken into account. Intensive efforts have been made in recent years on the development of processes for recycling and utilization of the waste catalyst materials as much as possible. Recovery of the valuable metals from the spent catalysts is an attractive option for their recycling and utilization. In the present work, the influence of ultrasonic agitation in enhancing the extraction of valuable metals such as Mo, V, and Ni from spent hydroprocessing catalysts by acid leaching was investigated. Two acids, one inorganic (H2SO4) and the other organic (citric acid), were used in the study. Citric acid was more active than H2SO4 for leaching metals from the spent catalyst. A comparison of the effectiveness of ultrasonic agitation and conventional mechanical stirring in the acid-leaching experiments conducted in the present study clearly demonstrated that ultrasonic vibration was more effective for the extraction of metals present in the spent catalyst. The leaching rate was enhanced by ultrasound, and large percentages (>95%) of all valuable metals (Mo, V, and Ni) present in the spent catalyst were extracted in a short time at a relatively low temperature (e.g., 60 °C) by combined use of citric acid and ultrasound. fetched_contents.text: Ultrasound-assisted oil removal of γ-Al2O3-based spent hydrodesulfurization catalyst and microwave roasting recovery of metal Mo Introduction As environmental issues have become increasingly prominent, environmental regulations on automotive fuel specifications and atmospheric emissions are moving toward more restrictive restrictions [1], [2], [3]. The petroleum refining industry needs a large amount of catalyst to purify and refine the oil. Catalysts deactivate over time as catalyst activity drops below acceptable levels. Generally, catalysts were regenerated and reused, however, regeneration was not always possible [4], [5]. This is because the catalysts used in these processes deactivate rapidly by coke, sintering and metal (V and Ni) deposits, leading to a short life [6]. After several cycles of regeneration and reuse, the activity of the catalyst is continuously reduced and further economically viable regeneration is not feasible. Spent catalysts are often discarded as solid waste [7]. On the other hand, with the increasing demand for hydrotreating catalysts, the mineral supplies become more and more insufficient to meet this demand [8]. Exploration of second resources, especially recovery of valuable metals from spent catalysts, is undoubtedly very important [9]. Spent hydrotreating catalysts typically contain about 20% oil, 4–12% Mo, 15–30% Al, and 0–4% Co or Ni [10], [11], which are extremely reusable to avoid wasting resources, economy loss and pollution of the environment. Recycling of Mo and Ni from wastes has improved the sources of metal elements, correspondingly reduced the need for mining and reduced the problem of discarding industrial waste. Oil-containing solid wastes are listed as hazardous wastes in the “List of national danger waste” (HW08term) due to the presence of hydrocarbons and aromatic hydrocarbons, which is an important factor that endangers the local environmental quality. According to the State Department's Regulations of “The fee collection statute for the waste discharge” (State Department Order No. 369), the cost of discharging one ton of oil-bearing solid waste is 1000 yuan. It is also a serious problem for an enterprise to discharge oily solid waste while destroying the environment. Therefore, an efficient treatment for oil-bearing solid waste is in urgent need for the development of the oil industry [12]. At present, many valuable studies have been conducted on the recovery of valuable metals from spent hydrotreating catalysts to reduce or eliminate environmental pollution [6], [10]. There are three main methods for treating waste hydrotreating catalyst: hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy and biological wet smelting [6], [13], [14], [15], [16]. Among these methods, the hydrometallurgical method is considered as a safer and more efficient method due to its unique advantages of simple operation, high metal recovery and low energy consumption [14]. Hydrometallurgical processes for the recovery of valuable metals from hydrotreated spent catalysts include leaching, separation of valuable metals, and product preparation [3]. Valuable metals could be completely or selectively dissolved in the leachate by leaching processes, such as acid leaching, alkali leaching and salt leaching [14], [17]. Then, according to the composition of the leachate, the metals can be separated by adsorption, ion exchange, precipitation, solvent extraction or molecular recognition [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23]. Finally, the products such as CoSO4 or NiSO4, CoC2O4, Al2O3, MoO3 and CaMoO4 can be successfully recovered from spent hydrotreating catalysts [20], [24], [25]. Despite the tremendous efforts made in recent years, some problems still exist for the industrial recovery of valuable metals from spent HDS catalysts. In traditional hydrometallurgical methods, the spent catalysts are initially roasted [26], in order to convert the metal sulfides to metal oxides or sulfates, and then subsequently leached using a strong base or strong acid [14]. First is roasting, which is simple and low-cost, but side effects still exist. The hardest part is the extreme flammable deflagration caused by uncontrolled temperatures [27], [28], [29]. The huge poisonous gas with incomplete combustion of oil has brought serious air pollution. Therefore, the most prominent problems become the deoiling process of spent HDS catalysts. And the oil cover on the surface will obstruct metal recycling during hydrometallurgical recovery. The other is extraction where organic solvents remove oil [30], [31], of which usually used are acetone, naphtha and toluene. However, because the solvent is toxic, although it can effectively remove oil, the industrial application of this method is still greatly hindered during the experiment. Based on the traditional extraction de-oiling process, Xu et al. [3] used anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and caustic soda (NaOH) to remove the oil substances on the spent catalyst surface. Leaching rate of Mo after baking in a muffle furnace for 1 h reached 98%. But SDS is toxic and NaOH is highly corrosive. Park et al. [14] roasted Mo-Ni/Al2O3 spent catalyst with H2SO4 followed by leaching of the baking mass concentrate. The disadvantages of this process are long baking time and utilization of corrosive H2SO4. In summary, the spent HDS catalyst pretreatment process consists of strong corrosive solvents, toxic and long baking time and other shortcomings. This not only resulted in high energy consumption and waste of resources, but also to the experimenter caused a permanent body injury. This study presented an ultrasonic-microwave assisted method for removal of oil and recovery of molybdenum from the spent MoNiCo/Al2O3 catalyst. The process parameters of ultrasonic-assisted oil removal were optimized using response surface methodology (RMS) to identify the optimum conditions. Mini-report on conventional leaching performance and its relevance as a baseline

Conventional leaching for spent HDS catalysts is described in the evidence as a standard hydrometallurgical route, with the spent catalysts typically leached in acidic media under appropriate conditions. The provided text states that “leaching spent catalysts in acidic medium under appropriate conditions leads to greater than 90% Mo, Al and Ni or Co extraction” [N1-F1]. This makes conventional acid leaching a strong baseline because it is often used to compare newer methods, and its reported extraction yields are reasonably high by the standards of hydrometallurgical recovery from spent catalysts [N1-F1].

A typical acid leaching environment is emphasized by the evidence as involving concentrated acids. The same source notes that “these procedures use concentrated acids, which require large amounts of reagents to neutralise the leaching solution” [N1-F1]. This points to a conventional operational pattern: strong acid leaching, usually with sulfuric acid or similar, and sometimes preceded by baking or oxidation steps, such as the example of “direct leaching with concentrated sulphuric acid and leaching with prior sulphuric acid baking” [N1-F1]. The evidence also explicitly states that “direct leaching with concentrated sulphuric acid and leaching with prior sulphuric acid baking” are examples of conventional approaches used for spent HDS catalysts [N1-F1]. It further notes that acid leaching is often combined with prior oxidation, such as “sulphuric acid leaching of a pre-oxidised catalyst” [N1-F1]. These details support a conventional baseline that is acidic, sometimes oxidative, and sometimes preceded by pretreatment baking.

For molybdenum extraction efficiency, the evidence reports that conventional acidic leaching can achieve greater than 90% Mo extraction [N1-F1]. However, this baseline is not without drawbacks. The same source states that these methods are “not selective,” and that alkaline leaching is used as an alternative to selectively extract Mo over Ni or Co [N1-F1]. In addition, conventional methods are criticized for requiring large amounts of reagents to neutralize the solution, which implies higher chemical and environmental costs [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that pyrometallurgical approaches are sometimes cheaper and faster, but they are impractical for low-grade catalysts because they produce harmful gases and require very high temperatures (>1,000 °C) [N1-F1]. While this comparison is not directly about conventional leaching, it helps situate conventional hydrometallurgy as a practical baseline with known tradeoffs.

The limitations of conventional leaching are clear from the evidence. First, it is not selective: concentrated acid leaching extracts Mo, Al, Ni, and Co together, and the text explicitly states that “the extraction is not selective” [N1-F1]. Second, the method is energy-intensive because it relies on concentrated acids and often requires baking or oxidation pretreatment [N1-F1]. Third, the evidence says that these methods require “large quantities of concentrated solutions” and “large amounts of reagents to neutralise the leaching solution” [N1-F1], which points to high chemical and waste-handling burden. Fourth, the text notes that conventional methods are less environmentally attractive than hydrometallurgy in some respects because they involve expensive reagents, slow reaction rates, and large quantities of concentrated solutions [N1-F1]. Taken together, conventional leaching is a useful baseline for Mo recovery from spent HDS catalysts, but it is limited by poor selectivity, high chemical demand, and energy-intensive pretreatment or reagent use [N1-F1].
node_outputs.N13:
Mini-report on spent HDS catalysts and process-specific factors

The major components of spent HDS catalysts that affect leaching are clearly identified in the evidence. The source states that the catalyst composition is mainly Al (15–30%), Mo (4–12%), Ni (1–5%), Co (0–4%), carbon, and sulphur [N1-F1]. The composition also depends on the original catalyst and the crude oil treated [N1-F1]. This is important because Al and Mo are the main metallic components, while carbon and sulphur are the main deactivating or residual species that complicate leaching [N1-F1]. The evidence further explains that spent catalysts are often covered with carbides, sulfides, and oily residues, giving considerable challenges in metal recovery [N3-R1]. This means that the presence of carbon, sulphur, and oil residues is a major leaching barrier, not just the metallic content itself [N3-R1].

Catalyst structure and particle size are also important. The evidence states that spent catalysts are deactivated by the deposition of carbon, sulphur, and metals such as V, Fe, Zn, and As [N1-F1]. It also notes that spent catalysts become solid wastes classified as hazardous materials [N1-F1]. The structural complexity is reinforced by the observation that catalysts often have oily residues and that spent catalysts are frequently covered with oil [N3-R1]. This implies that particle morphology and surface coverage are relevant to leaching, because oil residues can block metal access and complicate extraction [N3-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that spent catalysts contain 20% oil, 4–12% Mo, 15–30% Al, and 0–4% Co or Ni [N6-F3], which reinforces the idea that the physical structure and surface state are major factors in extraction performance.

Acid type, temperature, and solids-to-liquid ratio are all explicitly tied to process performance. The evidence repeatedly references acidic leaching as the conventional route, and it states that “leaching spent catalysts in acidic medium under appropriate conditions leads to greater than 90% Mo, Al and Ni or Co extraction” [N1-F1]. It also says that concentrated acids are used, and that the extraction is not selective [N1-F1]. This supports the conclusion that acid type matters greatly: concentrated acid leaching is common, but it is not inherently selective [N1-F1]. Temperature is another important variable, as the evidence notes that pyrometallurgical operations are usually faster but require extremely high temperatures (>1,000 °C) [N1-F1]. Although this is a pyrometallurgical rather than hydrometallurgical comparison, it shows that temperature is a major process factor that affects kinetics and feasibility [N1-F1].

Solids-to-liquid ratio is also relevant. The evidence reports that under optimized conditions, a molybdenum recovery of 87.36% ± 2.94 wt % was achieved using 1.3 M tartaric acid, 75 g/L solid–liquid ratio, and 60 min [N4-R3]. It also states that “the optimum leaching condition, giving 97% leaching efficiency, was determined to be 40 g×L⁻¹ sodium carbonate concentration, 2 h-leaching time” [N4-R4]. While these examples are not identical in chemistry, they both show that the solids-to-liquid ratio is a key operational parameter that can affect extraction efficiency and time [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: spent HDS catalysts are heterogeneous solids with a complex composition dominated by Al, Mo, Ni, Co, carbon, and sulphur, and leaching performance is heavily influenced by acid type, temperature, and solids-to-liquid ratio [N1-F1][N3-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4].
node_outputs.N10:
Mini-report on microwave-assisted leaching performance and advantages

Microwave-assisted leaching is presented in the evidence as a promising alternative to conventional leaching, especially for improving kinetics and reducing leaching time. The search result states that “microwave energy has considerable potential to enhance the efficiency of the leaching process and reduce the leaching time” [N5-R2], and that “it has been confirmed that microwave energy has considerable potential to enhance the efficiency of the leaching process and reduce the leaching time” [N5-R3]. This is a strong indicator that microwave-assisted leaching is generally more efficient and faster than conventional methods under many conditions [N5-R2][N5-R3].

The evidence also provides a direct efficiency comparison. In one study, under microwave-assisted conditions, Mo leaching reached 89% and 91% for Ni-Mo and Co-Mo catalysts, respectively [N5-R5]. This suggests that microwave-assisted leaching can achieve relatively high Mo extraction efficiencies, though the exact comparison with conventional leaching is not quantified in the provided evidence. However, the broader context is that microwave-assisted leaching is being investigated as an environmentally friendly technique to improve chemical reaction rates and reduce energy use [N1-F1][N5-R2]. The evidence also notes that hydrometallurgical processes are theoretically more environmentally friendly and use lower temperatures than pyrometallurgical methods [N1-F1], which places microwave-assisted leaching in a favorable environmental category relative to conventional high-temperature alternatives.

Microwave treatment improves kinetics and reduces leaching time through the mechanism of microwave heating. The evidence states that microwave-assisted acid digestion is commonly used for sample treatment and instrumental analysis, and that microwave radiation is an environmentally friendly technique [N1-F1]. More specifically, the literature cited in the search results describes microwave-assisted leaching as having considerable potential to enhance leaching efficiency and reduce leaching time [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence further notes that microwave energy has considerable potential to enhance the efficiency of the leaching process [N5-R2], which points to a mechanism of accelerated mass transfer and reaction kinetics rather than simply higher temperature. The exact physical mechanism is not spelled out in the provided evidence, but the repeated emphasis on enhanced efficiency and reduced time is consistent with microwave-induced heating and better contact between leaching solution and catalyst particles [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Selectivity effects and co-metal loss are also addressed in the evidence. The evidence states that conventional acid leaching is not selective, while alkaline leaching can be used to selectively extract Mo over Ni or Co [N1-F1]. The provided material does not directly report that microwave-assisted leaching is selective, so the evidence here is cautious: microwave-assisted leaching appears to improve efficiency and kinetics, but selectivity is not explicitly claimed in the supplied excerpts [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3].
